title: Small Case - An Airline Hedges Oil Prices
subtitle: Applying theory in practice: building a hedging strategy for fuel cost
openingQuestion: An airline expects to consume 10 million barrels of oil next year, at a current price of 70 USD/barrel. The CFO worries the price could rise to 90 USD. Which hedging strategy makes sense?
openingOptions: Buy futures or call options on oil to lock in part of the fuel cost near the current price, reducing risk if price rises sharply while keeping some flexibility
Do nothing, accept the risk fully
Raise airfares immediately to offset the risk in advance
explanation: A practical strategy: an airline usually hedges a certain percentage (e.g. 50-70%) of its expected fuel need with oil futures or call options, not hedging 100% so it can still benefit somewhat if the price falls. This is a balancing act between cost certainty and keeping some flexibility.

diagram.label: Still benefit partly if price falls

realWorldExample.description: Delta Air Lines once experimented with buying an entire oil refinery (Trainer Refinery) in 2012 to directly control its fuel cost - an extreme form of 'natural hedging' instead of only using financial derivatives.

quiz.question: Why do airlines usually not hedge 100% of their fuel need?
options: Because hedging everything at a high price becomes a disadvantage if the price of oil falls
Because aviation regulation caps the maximum hedge ratio
Because the cost of hedging everything exceeds the airline's profit
Because there aren't enough futures contracts available to cover the full need
quiz.explanation: Hedging is a double-edged sword: if you hedge everything at a high price and the market price then falls sharply, an unhedged competitor gains a much bigger cost advantage. So airlines usually only hedge part of their need, balancing protection from rising prices against not being at a competitive disadvantage if prices fall.

quiz.question: If the airline in this case hedged 60% of its fuel need at 70 USD/barrel, but the oil price then surges to 120 USD/barrel, what competitive advantage do they have over an unhedged rival?
options: They can resell the hedging contract for a financial profit
The regulator lets them raise fares before rivals do
They don't pay fuel tax during high-price periods
Much lower fuel cost, letting them keep airfares competitive
quiz.explanation: This is exactly the scenario where hedging proves its value most clearly: when material prices surge just as feared, the hedged portion helps the business avoid the full cost shock, giving a real competitive advantage over a rival with no hedging strategy.

quiz.question: Hedging 60% at 70 USD, market price rises to 120 USD. What is the average cost per barrel?
options: 120 USD (= the market price at the time of purchase)
70 USD (= the price locked in for the hedged portion)
95 USD (= the simple average of 70 and 120)
quiz.explanation: Weighted average: 42 + 48 = 90 USD. An unhedged competitor pays the full 120, so the 30 USD per barrel difference is a real cost advantage during the high-price period.

quiz.question: Why is Southwest Airlines famous for its oil-price hedging strategy?
options: Because they hold equity stakes in oil-drilling companies
Because they accurately predicted when the price of oil would surge
Because they are the only airline allowed to buy crude oil futures
Because they maintained disciplined hedging across many price cycles
quiz.explanation: The key is discipline, not fortune-telling: they hedge consistently according to policy, even in years when it caused a loss. That's why when the price surged, the cost advantage was already there, not down to luck.

quiz.question: What risk remains for an airline after hedging oil prices?
options: Jet fuel and crude oil don't move exactly in step
The hedging contract can be cancelled by the exchange during extreme moves
Airfares get capped by the regulator during high-price periods
The hedging cost is added to cost of goods sold, reducing profit margin
quiz.explanation: This is basis risk: the hedging instrument uses crude oil, while what the airline actually buys is refined jet fuel. The two prices move together but the gap between them still fluctuates.

keyTakeaways: Real-world hedging usually applies to only a percentage of the need, not 100%
Need to balance cost certainty against a competitive advantage if prices move favorably
A good hedging strategy is part of an overall competitive strategy, not just a pure financial decision

practicePrompt.question: An airline expects to consume 100 million liters of fuel next year, but only signs a hedging contract for 60 million liters, leaving 40 million liters exposed to market price movement. Why doesn't the airline hedge the full 100%?
options: This is a risk-management mistake, the airline should always hedge 100% of fuel needs to fully eliminate risk
Real-world hedging usually applies to only part of the need, not the full 100%
The airline doesn't hedge fully because hedging oil derivatives is illegal in some countries
The hedge ratio doesn't matter, having any hedging at all is enough to fully protect against price movement
practicePrompt.explanation: Real-world hedging usually applies to only a percentage of the need, not 100%. There's a balance to strike between cost certainty and a competitive advantage if prices move favorably - a good hedging strategy is part of an overall competitive strategy, not just a pure financial decision.

application.title: Design your own hedge ratio
application.message: Suppose you are an airline's CFO, decide what percentage of next year's fuel need you'll hedge (e.g. 50% or 70%) and explain why you didn't choose to hedge 100%.
application.secondary: There is no single correct answer - the goal is to practice thinking about risk trade-offs.

sections.text: Picture an airline planning next year's budget, knowing it will need a huge amount of fuel but not knowing where the price of oil will go. The practical strategy: hedge a certain percentage of expected need, not the entire amount.

If a business hedges its entire need at a fixed price and the price of oil then falls sharply, the company will completely lose its cost advantage compared with a rival that didn't hedge, or hedged less. So airlines usually only hedge 50-70% of their need using oil futures or call options, keeping the rest exposed so they can still benefit if the price falls - a balancing act between cost certainty and keeping competitive flexibility.
The rising-price scenario: hedging proves its value

Suppose the airline has hedged 60% of its fuel need at 70 USD/barrel, but the oil price then surges to 120 USD/barrel. Their average fuel cost will be much lower than a fully unhedged rival - especially important in an industry with thin profit margins like aviation, helping them keep either competitive fares or better profit during a period of high oil prices.

Delta Air Lines once experimented with buying an entire oil refinery (Trainer Refinery) in 2012 to directly control its fuel cost - an extreme form of 'natural hedging' instead of only using financial derivatives, showing hedging isn't limited to futures and options.

items: Real-world hedging usually applies to only a percentage of need (e.g. 50-70%), not the full 100%
Hedging everything at a high price can create a competitive disadvantage if price later falls sharply
When price rises exactly as feared, the hedged portion creates a clear cost advantage
A hedging strategy is part of an overall competitive strategy, not just a pure financial decision
